questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A rate used to support a claim about meaning
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a rate can support as a claim about meaning
questions.stem: In a translator's notes for a survey report, a rate is quoted to support the claim that readers found the wording clear, and the note asks what the rate can carry.

options.text: That the wording was rated clear by the respondents who answered, and not more than that.
That most readers of the original text find it clear, since a response rate speaks for a whole population.
options.misconception: confuses a response rate with a population-wide opinion

options.text: That the wording is clearer than a comparison text, because the rate is computed against a baseline.
options.misconception: assumes a rate implies a comparison that was never made

options.text: That the wording is clear, because a high rate of clear answers is the same as a high rate of clarity.
options.misconception: treats a response rate as a measure of clarity

questions.explanation: A response rate says how many people replied, not what they thought. The note can report the proportion of respondents who found the wording clear, but a claim about readers needs another basis.
questions.hint: Ask what the denominator of the rate actually is.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The generalisation a description does not license
questions.learningObjective: Explain the licence a description carries
questions.stem: A translator's note records that a description of one interview study is used to characterise a whole community, and asks for the explanation of the licence.

answer.exemplar: The interview study described how a small number of people in one setting talked about their work, and it said nothing about the distribution of views across the community. Characterising the community therefore borrows the description's vividness without its narrowness. The note should keep the study attached to its participants and say plainly that the wider picture was not studied.

questions.explanation: A description of a few people is a description of those people. Characterising a community borrows the detail but drops the narrowness that made it honest, so the note must name who was described.
questions.hint: Ask whose views the description actually reports.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Keeping a description at the level its warrant supports
questions.learningObjective: Hold a procedure description to its validated level

stimulus.body: A translator's note for a maintenance manual describes a calibration procedure that was validated on one family of instruments. The manual is sold for several families, and the note asks how far the validated procedure can be described as the method for all of them.

questions.stem: A calibration procedure was validated on one instrument family, and the note asks what the description may claim.

options.text: The procedure is the method for every family, because a validated procedure stays valid wherever it is used.
options.misconception: believes a validation follows the document, not the device

options.text: It is the validated procedure for the tested family, and the note must say which family that was.
The procedure is generic, so the note should drop the mention of instruments to keep the manual general.
options.misconception: believes generality is achieved by deleting the constraint

options.text: Nothing can be said, since a procedure validated on one family has no standing for any other family at all.
options.misconception: treats a bounded validation as worthless in every case

questions.explanation: Validation attaches a procedure to the things it was tried on. Writing it as the method for a whole range extends that attachment, so the note must name the family it was validated on.
questions.hint: Ask what the procedure was actually tried on.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Mechanism first, then evidence
questions.learningObjective: Order a result and a proposed mechanism in a note
questions.stem: Two notes disagree about whether a mechanism should be named before the numbers appear, and the editor asks for one combined principle.

options.text: Name the mechanism first, because a number without a cause leaves the reader unable to judge its weight.
options.misconception: treats a named cause as the source of evidential weight

options.text: Give the numbers first, because a mechanism introduced later is clearer to a reader who has the result.
options.misconception: believes ordering alone decides whether a claim is sound

options.text: State the result first, then the mechanism as a candidate that the evidence does not yet settle.
Leave the mechanism out, because naming a candidate cause invites readers to treat it as an established one.
options.misconception: removes a candidate mechanism to prevent misreading

questions.explanation: The notes answer different halves: what was observed, and what might explain it. Result first, mechanism second as a candidate the evidence does not settle, keeps each in its own place.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader may treat as established.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What counts as support for a mechanism claim
questions.learningObjective: Test whether a note's evidence supports its mechanism
questions.stem: First decide whether the note's evidence supports the mechanism it names, then say what the note must add if it does not.

options.text: It does support it, so the note must add a plain statement that the mechanism is now established.
options.misconception: announces a mechanism as settled on thin evidence

options.text: It does not support it, so the note must remove the mechanism and report only the observed effect.
options.misconception: deletes a candidate explanation instead of marking it

options.text: It supports it indirectly, so the note must add a paragraph setting out the reasoning that connects them.
options.misconception: treats an argument as if it were additional evidence

options.text: It does not support it, so the note must mark the mechanism as a proposal and say what would test it.

questions.explanation: Evidence that an effect occurred does not show which mechanism produced it, unless the design made the mechanism vary. The note keeps the mechanism as a proposal and says what would test it.
questions.hint: Ask what the design was able to vary.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Opposite results explained by a design difference
questions.learningObjective: Identify a design difference that could reverse a result
questions.stem: Two translated sources report opposite results for the same effect, and the translator's note asks what design difference could explain it.

options.text: The treatments were not the same in practice, so a reversal can sit inside a mechanism that is the same.
One source must be wrong, because two well-run studies of one effect cannot point in opposite directions.
options.misconception: assumes disagreement proves an error in one study

options.text: The translations differ, since opposing results usually come from a difference in how the text was rendered.
options.misconception: blames the translation for a difference in findings

options.text: The opposite results show the effect is not real, so the note should report that the question is settled.
options.misconception: treats disagreement as a verdict against the effect

questions.explanation: Opposite results are a prompt to look for a design difference, and the first candidate is the treatment in each case. Two studies can share a mechanism and still differ in dose or timing.
questions.hint: Ask what was done differently in each study.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Samples that differ behind the same phenomenon
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a difference between samples licenses
questions.stem: A translator's note compares two studies of the same phenomenon that used different samples, and asks for the explanation of what the difference licenses.

answer.exemplar: One study drew its participants from a hospital register and the other from a community roll, so the two groups differ in how ill they were and in what had already been tried. The rates are therefore estimates for two populations, not two estimates of one population, and the difference between them is information about the groups rather than a contradiction. The note can report both rates with their frames attached, and it cannot average them.

questions.explanation: Different samples give different populations, so the two rates answer two questions rather than one. The note reports each with its frame and refuses to pool them.
questions.hint: Ask what each sample was drawn from.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A rate used to support a claim about meaning
questions.learningObjective: Bind a rate to the group that produced it

stimulus.body: A translator's note for a product review attaches a satisfaction rate to the sentence that the service is easy to use. The rate came from a follow-up questionnaire sent to customers who had already complained about a delivery, which is a smaller and more dissatisfied group than the customers as a whole. The note asks what the rate can be attached to.

questions.stem: A satisfaction rate comes from a self-selected group, and the note asks what the rate can be attached to.

options.text: The service in general, because a rate of satisfaction describes the service rather than the respondents.
options.misconception: believes a rate describes the thing and not the group

options.text: That the complainants who answered were satisfied with the service, which is a separate and narrower claim.
Nothing, because a rate drawn from complainants is not evidence about satisfaction at all.
options.misconception: dismisses self-selected evidence as carrying nothing

options.text: The customers who were not asked, since those who replied did so precisely because they were dissatisfied.
options.misconception: infers the opposite group from the recruitment method

questions.explanation: The rate describes the people who answered, and answering was a selection that skewed the group. The note can report what those respondents said, while a claim about customers needs a fair sample.
questions.hint: Ask who was in a position to answer.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The generalisation a description does not license
questions.learningObjective: Combine a generalising note with a refusing note
questions.stem: A note generalises a described case to a national pattern while a second note refuses, and the editor asks how to combine them.

options.text: Keep the generalising note, because the detail of a case is what persuades a reader of a national pattern.
options.misconception: treats vivid detail as evidence of a wide pattern

options.text: Keep the refusing note, because a general claim is never warranted and the editor prefers the cautious text.
options.misconception: chooses caution without asking what the case can support

options.text: Keep the described case at its own level and mark the national claim as a claim the sources do not reach.
Split the difference with a hedged sentence that avoids both the case and the national pattern.
options.misconception: believes a vague sentence settles the level question

questions.explanation: The case and the pattern are different kinds of statement, and only one is what the sources describe. Combining the notes means keeping the case and marking the national claim as an addition.
questions.hint: Ask which sentence the source actually wrote.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Keeping a description at the level its warrant supports
questions.learningObjective: Fix a description level and mark the sentence above it
questions.stem: First fix the level at which the description is warranted, then mark the sentence in the draft that goes above it.

options.text: Warranted at the level of the region, so the sentence naming a single village is the one that goes above it.
options.misconception: assumes a regional description is the safe default level

options.text: Warranted only for one case, so every sentence describing a pattern, including the note itself, goes above it.
options.misconception: makes the note itself part of what must be rewritten

options.text: Warranted at the level of the source document, so any rewording in the draft goes above it.
options.misconception: ties the warrant to the wording of the original

options.text: Warranted for the single site described, so the sentence that generalises to the region is the one to fix.

questions.explanation: The level of a description is fixed by what the source covered, and marking an offending sentence depends on that. A one-site description can be faithful while a widening sentence is reworded.
questions.hint: Ask what the source actually covered.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Mechanism first, then evidence
questions.learningObjective: Order a result and a proposed mechanism in a note
questions.stem: A translator's note proposes a psychological mechanism to explain a flat result, and the editor asks what order the note should take.

options.text: Report the flat result first, then offer the mechanism as one candidate among several that fit it.
Open with the mechanism, since a reader who knows the explanation reads the number more carefully.
options.misconception: lets the proposed cause frame the reading of the result

options.text: Report only the flat result, because naming any mechanism invites the reader to overread the note.
options.misconception: suppresses a legitimate candidate explanation

options.text: Report the mechanism first, then the result, so the number appears as the confirmation of the idea.
options.misconception: arranges the order so the result reads as proof

questions.explanation: A result states what happened and a mechanism what might explain it, so the result comes first and the mechanism is a candidate. Opening with the mechanism frames the reading of the number.
questions.hint: Ask which part is observation and which is inference.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What counts as support for a mechanism claim
questions.learningObjective: Explain what repetition does and does not support
questions.stem: In a translator's notebook, a mechanism is claimed confirmed because two studies agree, and the note asks for the explanation of the support question.

answer.exemplar: Two studies agreeing tells the translator that both found the same effect and the same thing at the same time, which raises the reader's confidence that the effect is there. It says nothing about what produced it, because a mechanism is confirmed by seeing the effect appear when the mechanism is present and disappear when it is removed. Agreement is support for a result, and only a design that manipulated the mechanism can support the explanation.

questions.explanation: Agreement between studies supports the finding, since independent repetitions reduce the chance of a fluke. It leaves the mechanism untouched, because neither study varied the mechanism.
questions.hint: Ask what the studies actually varied.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Opposite results explained by a design difference
questions.learningObjective: Explain a reversal caused by a difference in definitions

stimulus.body: Two translated versions of a trial report describe the same control condition, and one says the control group improved while the other says it did not. The source notes in the translator's file record that the two reports used different definitions of improvement and different starting points for the comparison. The note asks how the disagreement should be handled.

questions.stem: Two trial reports disagree on whether a control condition helped, and the note asks how the difference is handled.

options.text: Report the more favourable result, since a translation should prefer the version that best serves the reader.
options.misconception: chooses a finding for its usefulness to the reader

options.text: Report each result with its own definition of improvement, since the designs differ in what they counted.
Report neither result, since two sources that define the same outcome differently cannot both be right.
options.misconception: treats a definitional difference as cancelling both findings

options.text: Report the disagreement without either result, since a note should describe a dispute rather than choose.
options.misconception: replaces the findings with a summary of the dispute

questions.explanation: Two reports that counted improvement differently answer different questions, so neither is wrong. The note reports each with its own definition and shows the comparison was never like for like.
questions.hint: Ask what each report counted as improvement.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Samples that differ behind the same phenomenon
questions.learningObjective: Draw the right conclusion from two differently sampled results
questions.stem: Two notes describe the same effect in populations that differ in recruitment, and the editor asks what the pair supports.

options.text: The effect exists in both groups, so it is general and the recruitment difference is beside the point.
options.misconception: treats a shared effect as proof of a shared population

options.text: The effect is real in one group only, so the note should keep the finding from the group that showed it.
options.misconception: assumes a difference in size means a difference in existence

options.text: The effect appears in both groups, and the size difference is evidence about the groups, not about the effect.
Nothing can be compared, since populations recruited differently cannot be placed side by side at all.
options.misconception: denies any comparison of differently recruited groups

questions.explanation: The same effect in two differently recruited groups supports the effect and tells you about the groups. Reading the size difference as evidence about the effect confuses one difference with another.
questions.hint: Ask what the difference between the groups is evidence of.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A rate used to support a claim about meaning
questions.learningObjective: Identify what an error rate can support
questions.stem: A translator's note uses an error rate to argue that a text is faithful to its source, and the editor asks what the rate can support.

options.text: That the text is a faithful rendering, because a low error rate measures faithfulness directly.
options.misconception: believes one number measures a whole quality

options.text: That the translation is better than the source, since fewer errors always mean a better text.
options.misconception: treats fewer errors as a judgement of overall quality

options.text: That the text contains no meaning changes, because errors of meaning were excluded from the count.
options.misconception: assumes a narrow error list covers every kind of change

options.text: That the counted errors were few, which is a statement about the count rather than about faithfulness.

questions.explanation: An error rate records only the errors the reviewer was looking for. The note can report how many were found and how they were defined, but faithfulness is a judgement the count cannot settle.
questions.hint: Ask what the reviewer was counting.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The generalisation a description does not license
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a small interview base licenses
questions.stem: A translator's note turns a description of three interview participants into a statement about a national audience, and asks for the explanation.

answer.exemplar: Three interviews can report how three people described their experience, and a translator may quote them accurately. They cannot establish what a national audience believes, because the note gives no account of how the three were selected and no basis for treating them as typical. The rewritten note keeps the three voices and drops the national framing, and it records that the wider claim was not supported by the source.

questions.explanation: Three interviews say nothing about who was chosen, so a national claim built on them describes a population never sampled. The note keeps the descriptions and names the general claim as an addition.
questions.hint: Ask how the three participants were chosen.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Keeping a description at the level its warrant supports
questions.learningObjective: Restore the level a softened sentence removed

stimulus.body: A translator's note for a plant manual describes a calibration routine in the general voice, without naming the instrument family it was developed for. The source text names the family once, in a sentence the translator softened. The note asks how the description should be worded.

questions.stem: A translator softened the sentence that named the instrument family, and the note asks how the description must be worded.

options.text: In the general voice, because a manual should not distract an operator with the limits of a method.
options.misconception: treats clarity as a reason to drop a method's conditions

options.text: With the family named and the routine marked as validated there, since the general voice borrows too much.
With the routine described as standard practice, since the source's named family is one of several in use.
options.misconception: upgrades a developed method into a general standard

options.text: Without the routine at all, because a method with a narrow scope serves no purpose in a plant manual.
options.misconception: removes the content rather than bounding the claim

questions.explanation: The general voice borrows authority a limited method lacks, and softening the sentence naming the family creates the gap. Naming the family and marking the routine as validated there keeps it honest.
questions.hint: Ask what the softened sentence was protecting.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Mechanism first, then evidence
questions.learningObjective: Order evidence and mechanism so the source stays distinct
questions.stem: A note explains a result by naming a mechanism, and a second note lists the evidence; the editor asks how to order them.

options.text: Mechanism first, so the reader knows what the evidence is for before the figures appear.
options.misconception: lets the proposed cause organise the evidence

options.text: Evidence first and mechanism second, with the mechanism marked as the reading the translators propose.
Evidence first and mechanism second, with the mechanism stated as the cause the evidence establishes.
options.misconception: promotes a candidate explanation into an established cause

options.text: Mechanism only, since the note's purpose is to explain the result rather than to record it.
options.misconception: treats the note as a commentary rather than a record

questions.explanation: The evidence is what the source recorded and the mechanism is the translators' reading of it, so the order must show that. Mechanism second, marked as a proposed reading, keeps the two distinct.
questions.hint: Ask which part came from the source.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What counts as support for a mechanism claim
questions.learningObjective: Test whether an unvaried mechanism is supported
questions.stem: First test whether the cited evidence could have produced the effect on its own, then state what the note must say.

options.text: It could, so the mechanism adds nothing and the note should report the effect without any explanation.
options.misconception: concludes that a mechanism can never be worth naming

options.text: It could not, so the note may report the mechanism as the confirmed explanation of the effect.
options.misconception: treats an unexplained remainder as proof of a mechanism

options.text: It could, so the note should mark the mechanism as one explanation among those the evidence cannot separate.
It could not, so the note should name a second mechanism, since two explanations narrow the field.
options.misconception: believes listing more mechanisms narrows the possibilities

questions.explanation: An effect the design can produce without the mechanism leaves it unexcluded, so it cannot be the explanation. Naming it as one candidate the evidence cannot separate is the strongest statement.
questions.hint: Ask what else the design could have produced.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Opposite results explained by a design difference
questions.learningObjective: Explain a reversal caused by different outcome measures
questions.stem: A translator's note encounters two studies with opposite findings and different outcome measures, and asks what explains the reversal.

options.text: The translation is at fault, because opposite findings usually mean one source was rendered badly.
options.misconception: blames rendering for a difference in study outcomes

options.text: One study was poorly conducted, so the note should prefer the result from the better designed source.
options.misconception: decides quality from the result rather than the design

options.text: The effect is unstable, so the note should report the result that has been replicated more often.
options.misconception: chooses a result by replication count, not comparability

options.text: The two studies measured different outcomes, so the results are not one effect in opposite directions.

questions.explanation: Opposite signs usually mean the studies are not measuring the same thing, and different outcome measures explain it without fault. The note checks comparability before calling it a contradiction.
questions.hint: Ask what each study actually measured.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Samples that differ behind the same phenomenon
questions.learningObjective: Explain why two accounts of one event differ
questions.stem: A translator's note places two accounts of the same event side by side, drawn from two quite different groups, and asks for the explanation of the comparison.

answer.exemplar: The first account was written by people who were present at the meeting and the second by people who read about it the following week, so the two describe different vantage points as much as different groups. Neither is a more accurate version of the event; each is accurate about what its authors could see and how they were placed. The note presents the two as two accounts, says who held each position, and refuses to merge them into a single scene.

questions.explanation: Two accounts of one event differ because their authors stood in different places, and the note must name each position. Merging them would hide the vantage point that shapes each.
questions.hint: Ask where each author was standing.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A rate used to support a claim about meaning
questions.learningObjective: Bound an incidence rate by where and when it was counted

stimulus.body: A translator's note for a public health report cites a per-thousand incidence figure in support of the sentence that the condition is rare in the region. The figure was calculated from a single year's hospital admissions in one district, and the district is not representative of the region. The note asks what the figure can be attached to.

questions.stem: An incidence rate from one district and one year is offered as evidence that a condition is rare, and the note asks what it shows.

options.text: The region as a whole, because an incidence rate is a property of a condition and not of where it was counted.
options.misconception: believes a rate is independent of the place counted

options.text: Nothing useful, because a rate computed from admissions counts only the people who reached a hospital.
options.misconception: dismisses a rate as useless because of incomplete capture

options.text: The district in that year, and any claim about the region needs evidence drawn from the region.
The region, provided the figure is rounded, since rounding smooths the difference between districts.
options.misconception: believes approximation removes a coverage difference

questions.explanation: The rate is a rate for the district and year it was counted, and it reflects only cases that reached a hospital. Calling the condition rare in the region needs evidence drawn from the region.
questions.hint: Ask where and when the rate was counted.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The generalisation a description does not license
questions.learningObjective: Bound a single site's practice to that site
questions.stem: A translator's note describes a single clinic's practice as the standard of care for the country, and the editor asks what it licenses.

options.text: A description of national practice, since one well-run clinic is a fair example of how care is given.
options.misconception: treats one site as a fair sample of a country

options.text: A description of that clinic, which becomes a national standard only if the note says it became one.
A general claim about care, because a practitioner who works that way shows how practitioners work.
options.misconception: generalises from one practitioner's practice to all

options.text: Nothing, because a single clinic's practice cannot be translated at all without national endorsement.
options.misconception: believes a description needs endorsement to be translatable

questions.explanation: One clinic's practice is evidence about that clinic, and calling it the national standard is a claim the note has not earned. The description stays faithful if the note leaves that status open.
questions.hint: Ask who else the description speaks for.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Keeping a description at the level its warrant supports
questions.learningObjective: Settle the level of a description against the source
questions.stem: A translator's note offers a general description, and a reviewer wants a specific one, and the editor asks how to settle the level.

options.text: Take the reviewer's version, since a specific description is always more informative for the reader.
options.misconception: prefers specificity regardless of what the source supports

options.text: Take the note's version, since a general description is safer and a specific one invites challenge.
options.misconception: chooses the general wording merely because it is safer

options.text: Match the level to what the source established, and mark any part where the note needed to be vaguer.
Offer both versions, since a general paragraph with a specific note gives the reader the choice.
options.misconception: presents two levels as a courtesy rather than a decision

questions.explanation: The level of a description is set by what the source established, not by a reader's preference. Where a translator must generalise, the note marks the place so the reader sees where it thins.
questions.hint: Ask what the source itself was prepared to say.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Mechanism first, then evidence
questions.learningObjective: Explain the gap between an effect and an asserted cause
questions.stem: A translator's note jumps from an effect to a cause without a mechanism, and asks for the explanation of the gap.

answer.exemplar: The source reports that an outcome changed and the translator's note asserts why, with no account of any process that would carry the effect from cause to outcome. A mechanism is that account, and without it the reader cannot judge whether the explanation would hold in the translated context, where the conditions may differ. The note either supplies the process in a form the reader can check, or it marks the cause as an interpretation the translators have added.

questions.explanation: Naming a cause without a process leaves the reader no way to check it where conditions differ. Supplying the process, or marking the cause as an addition, are the honest ways through.
questions.hint: Ask what process connects cause to outcome.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What counts as support for a mechanism claim
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish support for a result from support for a mechanism
questions.stem: The note for a translator claims a finding is confirmed because it appeared in two places, and the editor asks what counts as support.

options.text: Two independent repetitions support the result, and they say nothing about the mechanism that produced it.
Two repetitions confirm the mechanism, since the same cause operating in two places gives the same effect.
options.misconception: confuses repetition of a result with evidence for a cause

options.text: Two repetitions settle the question only if the two places share the same design, which the note does not say.
options.misconception: makes design similarity a requirement for simple repetition

options.text: Nothing supports the result, since repetition can only ever reflect a shared error in the source literature.
options.misconception: dismisses repetition as evidence because error is possible

questions.explanation: Repetition raises confidence that a result is real, since two independent findings are less likely an accident. It leaves the mechanism untouched, because neither repetition varied it.
questions.hint: Ask what the repetition varies.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Opposite results explained by a design difference
questions.learningObjective: Present two results whose comparison was confounded

stimulus.body: A translator's note compares two accounts of an intervention programme, one of which reports a clear improvement and the other a clear worsening. The source file records that the second programme gave the support service to a group that had already been receiving the first programme for a year. The note asks how the two results should be presented.

questions.stem: One programme's earlier support changes how a later comparison reads, and the note asks how to present both results.

options.text: Both results are reported as findings, because a note should not read design details into the sources.
options.misconception: avoids reading a design difference that the source records

options.text: The second result is reported with the first programme's history noted, because that history shaped it.
Only the first result is reported, because a comparison confounded by prior support is not interpretable.
options.misconception: discards a usable result instead of qualifying it

options.text: Both results are reported side by side with no comment, since the reader can check the sources for themselves.
options.misconception: leaves the reader to find the design difference unaided

questions.explanation: The second group had received the first programme, so the comparison was not between untouched groups. That history belongs beside the result, and reporting both without it invites a false read.
questions.hint: Ask what had already happened to the second group.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Samples that differ behind the same phenomenon
questions.learningObjective: Compare two rates computed on different samples
questions.stem: Two notes compare the same rate across two samples of different sizes and composition, and the editor asks what can be said.

options.text: The larger sample is the more accurate one, so the note should use its rate and discard the smaller.
options.misconception: judges accuracy by sample size and ignores composition

options.text: Both rates describe their own samples, and the difference between them is information about the samples.
The average of the two rates is the best estimate, because averaging draws on all the observations available.
options.misconception: believes averaging is legitimate when samples differ in kind

options.text: The smaller sample is the more informative one, because a smaller group is usually more carefully sampled.
options.misconception: believes small samples are more carefully drawn

questions.explanation: Two rates on differently composed samples describe two populations, and the gap between them says something about the populations. The note presents both with their frames.
questions.hint: Ask what the two samples have in common.

questions.topic: A rate used to support a claim about meaning
questions.learningObjective: Attach a meaning claim to the right rate
questions.stem: First decide what the rate is a rate of, then name the meaning claim the note may attach to it.

options.text: It is a rate of errors, so the note may attach the claim that the text is accurate in general use.
options.misconception: lets a rate of one thing become a claim about another

options.text: It is a rate of completed forms, so the note may attach the claim that customers find the form easy.
options.misconception: reads a completion rate as a judgement of difficulty

options.text: It is a rate of returns among people who bought, so the note may claim only what those buyers reported.
It is a rate of interest, so the note may attach the claim that readers engage closely with the material.
options.misconception: confuses a rate of interest with a measure of engagement

questions.explanation: A rate is always a rate of something, and that fixes the population it can describe. The note attaches its claim to the group the rate was computed over, which here is the buyers who returned an item.
questions.hint: Ask what lies under the numerator.

questions.topic: The generalisation a description does not license
questions.learningObjective: Identify the overreach in a prevalence claim from two informants
questions.stem: A translator's note reports what two informants said and generalises it to a belief held by the whole community.

options.text: The generalisation is fair, since two informants who agree show that the belief is widely shared.
options.misconception: treats informants' agreement as a measure of prevalence

options.text: The generalisation is fair, because the informants were chosen as knowledgeable about the community.
options.misconception: confuses expertise with representativeness

options.text: The generalisation is unfair, so the note must drop the informants' statements entirely from the translation.
options.misconception: discards usable material instead of narrowing the claim

options.text: The generalisation is unfair, because two informants cannot establish what a whole community believes.

questions.explanation: Two informants can report what they believe, and their agreement says little about how many hold the view. The note keeps the statements and drops the prevalence claim.
questions.hint: Ask how many people the note speaks for.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Keeping a description at the level its warrant supports
questions.learningObjective: Explain how paraphrase shifts a claim
questions.stem: A translator's note must choose how closely to paraphrase a source, and asks for the explanation of the level decision.

answer.exemplar: Paraphrasing a source trades two things: it lets a sentence sit in the register the reader expects, and it lets meaning shift in the direction of the new language. Close paraphrase keeps the claims attached to the people who made them, which is what a description of a few cases requires, and the translator's note records where a rendering could carry a different claim from the original. The level of detail is therefore set by what the source established and by who would be misinformed by a shift.

questions.explanation: Paraphrasing shifts a claim into the new language's expectations, so the note must know how far meaning may travel. The level is set by what the source established and by who a shift would mislead.
questions.hint: Ask who would be misled by a shift.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Mechanism first, then evidence
questions.learningObjective: Check whether evidence could show a proposed mechanism working
questions.stem: First name the mechanism the note is proposing, then check whether the evidence could show that mechanism working.

options.text: A change in incentives, and the evidence shows only the outcome, so the mechanism remains a proposal.
A change in incentives, and the outcome moved as the incentive changed, so the mechanism is supported.
options.misconception: reads a co-occurring change as proof the mechanism operated

options.text: The design of the note, and the evidence shows the outcome, so the note should keep the mechanism in the body.
options.misconception: treats the note's own construction as a candidate mechanism

options.text: A change in incentives, and the evidence cannot show it because the mechanism is unobservable in principle.
options.misconception: declares a mechanism unobservable and settles the argument

questions.explanation: A mechanism becomes supported when the design allowed it to vary and the outcome moved with it. Evidence showing only the outcome cannot separate it from everything else that changed alongside.
questions.hint: Ask what the design could make vary.

questions.topic: What counts as support for a mechanism claim
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a matched prediction supports a mechanism
questions.stem: A translator's note claims a mechanism because the outcome matched a prediction, and the editor asks whether that is support.

options.text: It is support, because a prediction that comes true is the strongest kind of confirmation available.
options.misconception: treats a successful prediction as decisive proof

options.text: It is not support, because a prediction matching an outcome is also what a wrong mechanism would produce.
It is support if the prediction was specific, since a specific prediction cannot be met by chance alone.
options.misconception: believes specificity alone rules out coincidence

options.text: It is not support, because the translators do not know which mechanisms the source had already excluded.
options.misconception: denies the note any basis for reasoning at all

questions.explanation: A prediction that comes true fits the mechanism and others that predict the same, so it singles out none. Support comes from designs in which the mechanism would have changed the outcome if absent.
questions.hint: Ask what else would have produced the same result.

questions.topic: Opposite results explained by a design difference
questions.learningObjective: Identify the design detail that flips a result's sign
questions.stem: A translator's note finds two replications pointing in opposite directions, and asks which design feature could flip the sign.

options.text: The number of languages the sources were translated into, since a rendering can subtly reverse an instruction.
options.misconception: believes translation direction can reverse a finding

options.text: The year the work appeared, since later work is always better designed than earlier work.
options.misconception: ranks studies by publication date instead of design

options.text: Which group was treated first, since reversing the order changes what a before and after comparison shows.
The size of the source team, since a larger team is more likely to report a reversal honestly.
options.misconception: credits honesty to team size rather than to design

questions.explanation: A before and after comparison reverses its sign when the group order is swapped, which happens when the later group receives the treatment the first had. That is the detail the note should look for.
questions.hint: Ask in which order the groups were treated.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Samples that differ behind the same phenomenon
questions.learningObjective: Explain what an identical headline number can hide
questions.stem: A translator's note sets two samples that produced the same headline number, and asks for the explanation of what the number hides.

answer.exemplar: The two figures agree because each is a rate computed over its own group, and the two groups differ in size, in the years covered and in how the cases were identified. A reader comparing the headlines would conclude that the two samples agree, when in fact they were never the same kind of thing. The note therefore keeps the denominators and the identification methods beside the numbers, because the agreement is between the labels rather than between the populations.

questions.explanation: Equal headline numbers can come from different groups, periods and counting methods, so agreement may be between labels, not populations. The note keeps denominators and methods beside the figures.
questions.hint: Ask what the two denominators were.

questions.topic: A rate used to support a claim about meaning
questions.learningObjective: Bind a response percentage to the respondents

questions.stem: A mail-back survey percentage is attached to a claim that readers found the material useful, and the note asks what it covers.

options.text: The subscribers who answered the request, since the percentage is a rate of responses within that group.
All readers of the material, because a percentage of responses generalises to the readers who stayed silent.
options.misconception: treats a response percentage as covering the non-responders

options.text: Nobody, because a mail-back survey cannot be used in a published review under any circumstances.
options.misconception: believes a survey method disqualifies a result entirely

options.text: The reviewers who wrote to complain, since complaints are the only readers whose answers are worth counting.
options.misconception: assumes only complainers are informative respondents

questions.explanation: The percentage is a rate within a group that chose to answer, and that choice is informative. The note attaches the figure to those subscribers; a claim about all readers needs a fair sample.
questions.hint: Ask who chose to answer the request.

questions.topic: The generalisation a description does not license
questions.learningObjective: Settle a case against a general claim in one wording
questions.stem: A note makes a general claim from one detailed case, and another note makes only a local claim, and the editor asks for one defensible wording.

options.text: Use the general claim, because the detailed case gives the general claim its evidence and colour.
options.misconception: treats one case as supplying evidence for a general claim

options.text: Use the local claim, because a general claim cannot be made from a case and the local one is enough.
options.misconception: believes the local claim is the only possible defence

options.text: Report the case in detail and mark the general claim as a reading the translator added for the reader.
Report both as alternatives, since a note that chose between them would be taking an editorial side.
options.misconception: avoids choosing because a note should stay neutral

questions.explanation: A case and a general claim are different statements, and one wording can carry only one honestly. The note reports the case as the source did and marks the general claim as a reading.
questions.hint: Ask what the source actually claimed.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Keeping a description at the level its warrant supports
questions.learningObjective: Explain what keeping a narrow level buys
questions.stem: A translator's note keeps a description at the level of a particular district, and the editor asks what that decision buys.

options.text: It buys speed, because a narrow description is quicker to read and quicker to check against the source.
options.misconception: justifies a level choice by editorial convenience

options.text: It buys accuracy, because a description that stays inside the source's scope is the one a reader can rely on.
It buys neutrality, because naming a district avoids the impression of endorsing any wider claim.
options.misconception: treats caution as a kind of neutrality

options.text: It buys reach, because a district-level description applies wherever the same conditions are found.
options.misconception: believes a narrow description transfers across places

questions.explanation: Staying inside the source's scope is what makes a description checkable against the source and reliable for a reader. Anything wider trades that accuracy for a reach the source never earned.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader can check the description against.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Mechanism first, then evidence
questions.learningObjective: Handle a mechanism note and an evidence note together
questions.stem: A translator's note has a mechanism without evidence and another has evidence without a mechanism, and the editor asks what must be added.

options.text: Add the mechanism to the evidence note, since an explanation is what makes a finding useful to a reader.
options.misconception: assumes an explanation needs no support of its own

options.text: Add the evidence to the mechanism note, since a claim without data should simply be removed or backed.
options.misconception: treats backing an assertion as a substitute for checking it

options.text: Mark what each note has, so the reader sees the mechanism is unevidenced and the result unexplained.
Merge the two notes, since a mechanism and a result belong together in a single account of the study.
options.misconception: joins an unsupported mechanism to a supported result

questions.explanation: A mechanism without evidence and a result without a mechanism are two gaps, and merging them hides both. Marking what each note has shows that one reading is proposed and one finding recorded.
questions.hint: Ask what each note can be relied on for.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What counts as support for a mechanism claim
questions.learningObjective: State what evidence and mechanism each contribute
questions.stem: First state what the note's evidence can establish, then state what the mechanism adds to the claim.

options.text: The evidence establishes the result and the mechanism establishes the cause, so the claim becomes causal.
options.misconception: lets a named mechanism convert a result into a cause

options.text: The evidence establishes the mechanism, and it adds the explanation the reader needs for the result.
options.misconception: swaps the roles of the evidence and the mechanism

options.text: The evidence establishes the result, and the mechanism adds nothing until a design is found that varied it.
options.misconception: lets an unvaried mechanism support a causal claim

options.text: The evidence establishes the result, and the mechanism marks a reading of it that the evidence leaves open.

questions.explanation: A note must keep the two jobs apart: the evidence supports the result and the mechanism is a reading of it. What the mechanism adds is a way of understanding the result, not a cause.
questions.hint: Ask what each part of the note is doing.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Opposite results explained by a design difference
questions.learningObjective: Present two trial results with their dose and timing

stimulus.body: A translator's note compares two translated trials of the same medicine. One reports that the treatment reduced symptoms, and the other reports that it increased them. The source records show that the second trial gave half its participants a lower dose than the first trial used, and that the two trials measured symptoms at different times after dosing. The note asks how the disagreement should be presented.

questions.stem: Two trials of one medicine disagree, and the note asks how the design differences should be presented.

options.text: Each result with the dose and timing behind it, since the treatments and measurements were not the same.
The result from the larger trial, since a larger trial is by definition the better designed one.
options.misconception: judges a study by size instead of by design

options.text: The result that matches the source's own conclusion, since the translator should follow the source's summary.
options.misconception: lets the source's summary choose between findings

options.text: Neither result, since a disagreement between trials of one medicine means the question is still open.
options.misconception: turns a design difference into an open scientific question

questions.explanation: A lower dose and a different measurement time mean the trials did not observe the same thing, so they are not two verdicts on one question. Each result belongs with its dose and timing.
questions.hint: Ask what dose was given and when it was measured.

questions.topic: Samples that differ behind the same phenomenon
questions.learningObjective: Conclude correctly from two different group figures
questions.stem: A translator's note reports the same phenomenon from two groups and the numbers differ, and the editor asks what to conclude.

options.text: That the phenomenon varies between groups, since two different numbers are two different truths about it.
options.misconception: treats group differences as properties of the phenomenon

options.text: That the two reports describe different populations, so the numbers are estimates for different things.
That the smaller number is the more accurate one, since a larger group usually measures more carefully.
options.misconception: believes a smaller group produces a more accurate estimate

options.text: That one source is unreliable, since two accounts of one phenomenon cannot both be accepted.
options.misconception: makes disagreement a verdict on one source

questions.explanation: Different numbers for one phenomenon usually reflect different groups, and saying so lets a reader use both reports. Calling one unreliable needs evidence the note lacks.
questions.hint: Ask which groups the two reports describe.

options.text: That the form is easy, because most people who started it also finished it.
options.misconception: reads a completion rate as a measure of difficulty

options.text: That the form is easy for everyone, since the completion rate applies to every user of the form.
options.misconception: assumes a completion rate covers every user

options.text: That most people who began the form finished it, which is a fact about starting and not about ease.
That the form is short, since a high completion rate is only possible when there is little to fill in.
options.misconception: believes completion rate measures the length of a form

questions.explanation: A completion rate says how many who started went on to finish, and those who abandon may differ in why. It supports a statement about starting and finishing; a claim about ease needs effort.
questions.hint: Ask who is not in the completion rate.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The generalisation a description does not license
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a headline generalisation licenses
questions.stem: A translator's note borrows a headline generalisation from a press release, and asks for the explanation of what it licenses.

answer.exemplar: A press release states the finding as a general fact about a population, because that is the form a headline takes. The underlying study observed a particular group under particular conditions, and the translators are handed only the finished generalisation, with the sample and the conditions stripped away in the process. Carrying it into a book reproduces the release's claim, so the note has to mark where the widening happened and what the study actually covered.

questions.explanation: A headline is already a widened claim, and copying it copies the widening rather than the evidence. The note has to mark what the study covered so the reader can see how much the release added.
questions.hint: Ask what the release removed from the finding.

questions.topic: Keeping a description at the level its warrant supports
questions.learningObjective: Attach a bench result to the grade and loading tested

questions.stem: A bench result is paraphrased into a general statement about a material, and the note asks how to word it.

options.text: As a general statement, because a bench test on one grade still characterises the material as a whole.
options.misconception: believes a single-grade result characterises the material

options.text: With the grade and loading named, so the statement stays attached to what was actually tested.
As a general statement with the word apparently in front, which is enough to show the claim is approximate.
options.misconception: believes a hedge word repairs a widened claim

options.text: As a general statement with the laboratory named, since naming the source makes the claim safe to repeat.
options.misconception: believes naming a source licenses the scope of the claim

questions.explanation: A result on one grade and one loading pattern attaches to that grade and pattern, and a general statement detaches it. Naming both keeps the claim attached to what was tested.
questions.hint: Ask what was actually loaded and measured.

options.text: Name the cause first, because a reader who knows the mechanism interprets the correlation correctly.
options.misconception: lets a cause set the reading of an observed association

options.text: Report only the correlation, because naming a cause in a note is the same as asserting it.
options.misconception: treats mentioning a cause as asserting it

options.text: Name the cause and the correlation together, since a pair of statements reads as a single supported claim.
options.misconception: believes adjacency turns two statements into one claim

options.text: Report the correlation first, then the cause as a reading the note has added and the source did not state.

options.misconception: treats any designed comparison as settling a question

options.text: Weight the plausible story more, because the mechanism was worked out in detail and the test was indirect.
options.misconception: prefers a detailed rationalisation over a direct test

Weight them equally, since a mechanism that fits the result and one tested in a trial are one kind of claim.

options.misconception: asserts that translation error is the usual explanation

options.text: Only after the designs are checked, since a design difference is likelier and translation error comes last.
No, because a translator can never detect a reversal in a technical comparison without changing the meaning.

options.text: No, because opposite findings in the literature are a normal and unremarkable feature of research.
options.misconception: treats disagreement as unremarkable and so uninformative

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Keeping a description at the level its warrant supports
questions.learningObjective: Explain what compression removes from a qualified account
questions.stem: A translator's note compresses a long qualified account into one sentence, and asks for the explanation of what the compression removes.

answer.exemplar: The source account qualifies nearly every claim, saying that the practice was uneven, that the sample was partial, and that the conditions varied from site to site. A single sentence can carry the subject and the main point, but each of those qualifications occupies a clause that has nowhere to go when the sentence is compressed. The note therefore keeps the sentence short and names the dropped qualifications, so a reader knows that the shortness is a rendering choice rather than a settled fact.

questions.explanation: Compression keeps the assertion and drops the hedges, and those hedges often carry the source's limits. Naming them shows the reader that the plainness of the sentence is a choice, not a fact.
questions.hint: Ask which qualifiers no longer fit.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Mechanism first, then evidence
questions.learningObjective: Place a translator's own mechanism after the source finding

stimulus.body: A translator's note explains a drop in reported incidents by naming a change in how staff recorded them, and the source text gives the same drop with no explanation at all. The note adds the recording change as the translator's own inference. The editor asks what the note must show first.

questions.stem: A note supplies a mechanism the source did not give, and the editor asks what must come first in the note.

options.text: The mechanism, because a note exists to make the source intelligible and an unexplained drop is not.
options.misconception: assumes a note may supply an explanation on its own

options.text: The recorded drop, so the reader sees the finding before the translator's reading of it.
The recording change, since the mechanism is what the reader came to the book for and the figure is secondary.
options.misconception: puts the translator's inference ahead of the source finding

options.text: Both together, since a drop and its explanation in one sentence is clearer than either on its own.
options.misconception: merges a source finding with a translator's inference

questions.explanation: A translator's mechanism is an addition, and an addition placed before the finding borrows the finding's authority. Reporting the drop first, then the reading as an inference, keeps them separable.
questions.hint: Ask which part the source itself supplied.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What counts as support for a mechanism claim
questions.learningObjective: Weigh a pattern match as support for a mechanism
questions.stem: A translator's note argues a mechanism is established because the effect appeared where it should, and the editor asks about the warrant.

options.text: The warrant is adequate, since the effect appearing in the predicted place is what a mechanism means.
options.misconception: treats a predicted pattern as a complete test of a mechanism

options.text: The warrant is adequate, since the note also cites a second study in which the effect was absent.
options.misconception: accepts an absence as confirmation of a mechanism

options.text: The warrant is thin, because other mechanisms would give the same pattern and the note has not separated them.
The warrant is thin, because a mechanism can only be established in a laboratory and never in a note.
options.misconception: believes confirmation belongs to laboratories alone

questions.explanation: A mechanism that predicts where the effect appears is consistent with the data, and consistency is not establishment. Other candidates predicting the same pattern are what the note must acknowledge.
questions.hint: Ask what else would produce the same pattern.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Opposite results explained by a design difference
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a treatment reversal does to a comparison
questions.stem: A translator's note meets two studies whose results disagree because one reversed the treatment, and asks what the design difference means.

options.text: Nothing, since reversing the treatment is a routine step that leaves the comparison intact.
options.misconception: believes a reversal cannot change what a study finds

options.text: That the second study is weaker, because reversing the treatment is a less common way to work.
options.misconception: judges a design by its popularity rather than its logic

options.text: That the two studies were measuring the effect in opposite directions, so the effect is inherently unstable.
options.misconception: reads a design difference as instability in the effect

options.text: That the two studies answer different questions, because who gets the treatment first decides the comparison.

questions.explanation: Reversing the treatment changes what a before and after comparison measures, so the studies estimate different quantities. Recognising this lets a note present both without implying a reversal.
questions.hint: Ask who received the treatment first.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Samples that differ behind the same phenomenon
questions.learningObjective: Explain what two registers of one city permit

stimulus.body: A translator's note compares two samples of the same city. One sample was drawn from the electoral register and the other from the register of people who had used a particular service, and the reported rate for the second sample is much higher than for the first. The note asks what the comparison permits.

questions.stem: Two samples of one city come from different registers, and the note asks what the comparison permits.

options.text: Nothing beyond saying the service users show a higher rate, since the two registers describe different groups.
That the city as a whole has the higher rate, because the users are part of the city and a part sets it.
options.misconception: treats a subgroup rate as the rate for the whole city

options.text: That the service raises the rate, since the people who used it are the ones who show the higher figure.
options.misconception: reads a selection effect as a causal effect

options.text: That the electoral register gives the true rate, because a general register is always more reliable.
options.misconception: ranks registers by generality rather than by fit

questions.explanation: A service register is a selected group, so the higher rate may reflect who signed up rather than the service's effect. The note reports the figures with their frames and claims neither about the city.
questions.hint: Ask what made the second group different.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A rate used to support a claim about meaning
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limit of a reading-speed rate
questions.stem: A translator's note supports a claim about how readable a text is with a reading-speed rate, and asks for the explanation of the limit.

answer.exemplar: A reading-speed rate says how fast a particular set of readers moved through a particular text, and it depends on the difficulty of the wording, the subject matter and the reader's familiarity. It is a measure of an activity, not a measurement of a property of the language. The note can report the rate and what it was measured under, and the claim about readability has to rest on something that captures the effort the readers spent, such as how often they had to go back.

questions.explanation: A rate of reading measures an activity under particular conditions, not a fixed property of the text, and familiarity moves it. A readability claim needs evidence about effort, not speed.
questions.hint: Ask what else besides wording moves the rate.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The generalisation a description does not license
questions.learningObjective: Combine a widened note with a narrow one
questions.stem: A note generalises a description of a village to a region and a second note stops at the village, and the editor asks how to combine them.

options.text: Keep the generalising note, since the regional statement is what the chapter covers and the village a detail.
options.misconception: lets a chapter's subject decide the level of a claim

options.text: Keep the village description and mark the regional claim as a reach the sources did not establish.
Keep the village description and drop the regional claim, because a note should never carry a general reading.
options.misconception: refuses to acknowledge a reading the reader will form anyway

options.text: Keep both as parallel sentences, so a reader wanting the regional reading can take it and another ignore it.
options.misconception: presents two levels without saying which the sources support

questions.explanation: The two notes differ only in reach, and the source fixes the reach evidence can carry. Reporting the village as described, and marking the regional version as an unestablished reach, keeps the limit.
questions.hint: Ask how far the source's own reach went.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Mechanism first, then evidence
questions.learningObjective: Handle two candidate mechanisms in a note
questions.stem: A translator's note names two candidate mechanisms for one result and settles on neither, and the editor asks what the note must do.

options.text: Pick one, because a note that names no mechanism gives the reader nothing to hold onto.
options.misconception: prefers decisiveness over accuracy

options.text: Remove both, because an undecided mechanism is the same as no mechanism and clutters the note.
options.misconception: removes content to tidy the note

options.text: Name both as candidates and say which observation would separate them, since the source leaves that open.
Add a third, because more candidate mechanisms make the note a more complete account of the field.
options.misconception: believes more candidates make a note more complete

questions.explanation: Two candidates that both fit the result leave an open question, and the useful addition is the observation that would separate them. Choosing one would put an unsupported preference in the note.
questions.hint: Ask what would distinguish the two candidates.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Samples that differ behind the same phenomenon
questions.learningObjective: State the comparison two differently drawn samples permit
questions.stem: First establish which samples the two notes describe, then state the comparison the note may make.

options.text: Both describe the same group at two points in time, so the note may report the change between them.
options.misconception: assumes two samples of one group form a time series

options.text: One describes a city and one a district, so the note may report the district figure as the smaller scale.
options.misconception: reads a scale difference as a comparison of values

options.text: One describes volunteers and one a random sample, so the note may report the random sample and drop the other.
options.misconception: drops a group on the strength of how it was recruited

options.text: They describe different groups, so the note may compare them only as two estimates of separate populations.

questions.explanation: Identifying the samples first tells the translator what comparison is possible, and two differently drawn groups are two estimates. The note reports both and states the limit of the comparison.
questions.hint: Ask how each group was drawn.
